profile.name: Jeremy Lim
profile.bio:
I am Jeremy Lim, an undergraduate at International Christian University in Tokyo, studying Linguistics and Information Science. My academic interests center on computational linguistics, speech science, and low-resource language research, especially Southern Min (Hokkien).

Beyond research, I am involved in photography, writing, and interdisciplinary collaboration. I am interested in how faith, technology, and human dignity interact in the age of AI.

christian.title: Christian
christian.lead: Faith is not one interest among others for me. It is the thing that reorganised everything else.
christian.body:
I came to faith at fourteen, at a point where I could not find a reason for my own life, and was baptised in 2023. What changed was not that my circumstances improved but that my worth stopped depending on them — I was loved for existing rather than for achieving, and that is still the thing I return to.

At ICU I try to put that into practice rather than only hold it privately. I served at Worship Night in 2025, and since 2025 I have hosted the Alpha Course, which is a space for people with genuine questions rather than settled answers. In 2026 I organised the Faith × Research Symposium during C-Week, because I do not think faith and academic work belong in separate rooms.

My sense of calling is toward East Asia — translation of scripture into low-resource languages, reconciliation between Japan and China, and unity across churches. I hold that loosely. It is a direction, not a plan.

linguist.title: Linguist
linguist.lead: I work on the sounds of a language that most people who speak it were told not to write down.
linguist.body:
I study Linguistics and Information Science at International Christian University, and from 2026 to 2027 I will be on exchange at the University of Edinburgh's School of Informatics. My work sits between phonetics, speech science and machine learning.

Most of my research is on Southern Min — Hokkien, Taiwanese — and specifically its checked tones: the abrupt syllables ending in /k/, /p/, /t/ and a glottal stop. They form a clean contrast in the phonology, but acoustically the cues are scattered across duration, formant transitions, energy decay and voice quality, which makes them a good test of what is actually separable in the signal. I presented that work at HIS PhonCog 2026, comparing machine classification against how listeners from five language backgrounds hear the same contrasts.

I came to this partly through Hokkien being a language of my own background, and partly because low-resource languages are where the interesting problems are — there is no large corpus to fall back on, so you have to think carefully about what the data can and cannot support.

photographer.title: Photographer
photographer.lead: Mostly quiet things: light through trees, a mountain behind power lines, a campus in snow.
photographer.body:
I photograph what I walk past. Very little of it is staged — it is mostly Tokyo and the places I travel to, taken on the way to somewhere else.

What I look for is ordinary scenes that hold still for a moment: morning light on a wooden hut, cherry blossom over a bicycle rack, Fuji framed by tangled wires. I like the wires. A photograph of the mountain alone is a postcard; the wires make it a place where someone actually lives.

I shoot digital and work in natural light almost entirely.

writer.title: Writer
writer.lead: Essays and papers across faith, language, education and East Asia — in English, Japanese and Chinese.
writer.body:
I write in three languages, and what I write splits roughly three ways.

There are testimonies and talks given at church and at ICU chapel — the most personal things here, and the ones I was most hesitant to publish. There is academic work: phonology and phonetics papers, a syntax report, and a study on what shapes students' openness to worldviews other than their own. And there are essays on things I keep returning to — China's education system and what cramming does to children, Chinese residents in Japan and how they are seen, the ethics of language policy when a state decides which languages count.

The common thread is probably that I am interested in what happens to people at the edges of systems — of an education system, of a language policy, of a society's idea of who belongs.
